cases.excerpt: In this study, we analyzed the effect of Turkish coffee and black tea consumption, alcohol intake and smoking on bladder cancer. A total of 164 patients with bladder tumors and 324 individuals without primary tumors were included in the study.

validated_results.title: Alcohol drinking and renal cell carcinoma in Canadian men and women.
authors: Canadian Cancer Registries Epidemiology Research Group
validated_results.reason: Population-based case-control study reporting sex-specific odds ratios for total alcohol intake and incident renal cell carcinoma.

extraction.comparison_type: highest intake group (>=22.3 g/day) versus non-drinkers
extraction.population: newly diagnosed histologically confirmed RCC cases and population controls in eight Canadian provinces

sample_size.excerpt: The present study examines the association between alcohol intake and the risk of RCC among men and women. Mailed questionnaires were completed by 1138 newly diagnosed, histologically confirmed RCC cases and 5039 population controls between 1994 and 1997 in eight Canadian provinces.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 1138 + 5039 = 6177

cases.excerpt: Mailed questionnaires were completed by 1138 newly diagnosed, histologically confirmed RCC cases and 5039 population controls between 1994 and 1997 in eight Canadian provinces.

effect_size.excerpt: Total alcohol intake was inversely associated with RCC in men and in women; the OR for the highest intake group (> or =22.3 g/day among men and > or =7.9 g/day among women) versus the non-drinkers was 0.7 (95% CI, 0.5-0.9) for both sexes.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Total alcohol intake was inversely associated with RCC in men and in women; the OR for the highest intake group (> or =22.3 g/day among men and > or =7.9 g/day among women) versus the non-drinkers was 0.7 (95% CI, 0.5-0.9) for both sexes.

comparison.excerpt: the highest intake group (> or =22.3 g/day among men and > or =7.9 g/day among women) versus the non-drinkers

timing.excerpt: A food frequency questionnaire provided data on eating habits and alcohol consumption 2 years before data collection.

continent.excerpt: between 1994 and 1997 in eight Canadian provinces

exposure_measurement.excerpt: A food frequency questionnaire provided data on eating habits and alcohol consumption 2 years before data collection.

gender.excerpt: Alcohol drinking and renal cell carcinoma in Canadian men and women.

smoking_status.excerpt: Smoking and obesity were not important effect modifiers.

validated_results.title: Meat and fish consumption and cancer in Canada.
authors: Canadian Cancer Registries Epidemiology Research Group
validated_results.reason: Case-control study of incident histologically confirmed bladder cancer reporting a direct association with processed meat intake, although no bladder-specific numeric estimate appears in the abstract.

extraction.comparison_type: higher versus lower processed meat intake (categories not specified in abstract)
extraction.population: incident histologically confirmed cancer cases and population controls in 8 Canadian provinces

sample_size.excerpt: Mailed questionnaires were completed by 19,732 incident, histologically confirmed cases of cancer of the stomach, colon, rectum, pancreas, lung, breast, ovary, prostate, testis, kidney, bladder, brain, non-Hodgkin's lymphomas (NHL), and leukemia and 5,039 population controls between 1994 and 1997 in 8 Canadian provinces. Measurement included information on socioeconomic status, lifestyle habits, and diet.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 19732 + 5039 = 24771

effect_size.excerpt: Total meat and processed meat were directly related to the risk of stomach, colon, rectum, pancreas, lung, breast (mainly postmenopausal), prostate, testis, kidney, bladder, and leukemia.

validated_results.title: Plasma vitamins E and A and risk of bladder cancer: a case-control analysis.
validated_results.reason: Case-control study reporting adjusted odds ratios for plasma retinol (vitamin A) and bladder cancer risk.

extraction.comparison_type: highest versus lowest quartile of plasma retinol
extraction.population: bladder cancer patients and age-, gender-, and ethnicity-matched controls

sample_size.excerpt: 386 bladder cancer patients and 389 age-, gender-, and ethnicity-matched controls were included in the study.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 386 + 389 = 775

cases.excerpt: 386 bladder cancer patients and 389 age-, gender-, and ethnicity-matched controls were included in the study.

effect_size.excerpt: Increased retinol level was also associated with reduced risk with OR of 0.57 (95% CI: 0.40-0.81). The ORs and 95% CIs for the second, third, and fourth quartiles were 0.92 (0.61-1.39), 0.66 (0.43-1.01), and 0.62 (0.40-0.95), respectively, with significant dose-response trend (P for trend = 0.01).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Increased retinol level was also associated with reduced risk with OR of 0.57 (95% CI: 0.40-0.81). The ORs and 95% CIs for the second, third, and fourth quartiles were 0.92 (0.61-1.39), 0.66 (0.43-1.01), and 0.62 (0.40-0.95), respectively, with significant dose-response trend (P for trend = 0.01).

comparison.excerpt: In quartile analysis, using subjects with the lowest alpha-tocopherol level as the reference group

design.excerpt: Plasma vitamins E and A and risk of bladder cancer: a case-control analysis.

timing.excerpt: Epidemiologic data were collected via in-person interview.

exposure_measurement.excerpt: Plasma concentrations of alpha-tocopherol, gamma-tocopherol, and retinol were determined by a high-performance liquid chromatography assay.

extraction.p_value_method: two-sided Wald test from effect and 95% CI on the log scale
extraction.ethnicity_basis: Default: no protocol-mapped specific country or population was established

validated_results.title: Plasma vitamins E and A and risk of bladder cancer: a case-control analysis.
validated_results.reason: Case-control study reporting adjusted odds ratios for plasma alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E) and bladder cancer risk.

extraction.comparison_type: highest versus lowest quartile of plasma alpha-tocopherol
extraction.population: bladder cancer patients and age-, gender-, and ethnicity-matched controls

effect_size.excerpt: In quartile analysis, using subjects with the lowest alpha-tocopherol level as the reference group, the adjusted ORs and 95% CIs for the second, third, and fourth quartiles were 0.75 (0.50-1.14), 0.69 (0.46-1.05), and 0.50 (0.32-0.78), respectively (P for trend = 0.003). Increased retinol level was also associated with reduced risk with OR of 0.57 (95% CI: 0.40-0.81).
